concepts.mechanism_summary: The shape-memory effect results from a thermoelastic martensitic transformation — a reversible, diffusionless transformation between two crystal microstructures (high-temperature austenite and low-temperature martensite). When the alloy cools below the martensite start temperature, a shear-like mechanism causes the lattice to transform without atomic diffusion; the martensitic phase self-accommodates by forming multiple twin variants that minimise strain. When mechanically loaded, those twins de-twin (reorient) under stress, causing macroscopic deformation. On reheating above the austenite finish temperature, the reverse transformation restores the original crystal structure and recovers the original shape. The transformation is thermoelastic: the phase boundaries are glissile and the transformation is fully reversible with a small thermal hysteresis.

atoms.verbatim_quote: a reversible, diffusionless transformation between two different crystal microstructures that occurs when the alloy is heated or cooled beyond alloy specific transition temperatures
atoms.mechanism_atom: Thermoelastic phase switch: diffusionless lattice shear converts austenite to martensite upon cooling and reverses fully on heating, recovering original shape.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the martensitic phase forms many twins in a process called self-accommodating twinning, and when the martensite is loaded, these self-accommodating twins provide an easy path for deformation
atoms.mechanism_atom: Under mechanical load, self-accommodating twin variants reorient (de-twin) preferentially, accommodating macroscopic strain without dislocation slip; heat-driven reverse transformation then restores shape.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the martensite formation is explained by a shear mechanism or sequence of two shear mechanisms, which can take place either by twinning or by sliding
atoms.mechanism_atom: Sequential shear steps (twinning or sliding) store geometric information in the crystal; the reverse shear on heating recovers the pre-deformation geometry with high fidelity.

Capillary Bridging as a Tool for Assembling Discrete Clusters of Patchy Particles

concepts.mechanism_summary: A capillary bridge forms when a liquid meniscus spans the gap between two solid surfaces, creating an adhesive force. The force has two components: (1) direct surface tension acting along the contact line (always attractive), and (2) a hydrostatic Laplace pressure term arising from the meniscus curvature (attractive for concave bridges, repulsive for convex). The net capillary force depends critically on the bridge volume, the surface separation, contact angles, and the Young-Laplace curvature of the free surface. When the surfaces are pulled apart beyond a critical rupture distance, the bridge breaks. Capillary bridging drives cohesion in wet granular media (sandcastles) and enables particle self-assembly into clusters.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the capillary force exerted on solid particles due to the liquid bridge is the sum of two components: contributions from the surface tension and the hydrostatic pressure
atoms.mechanism_atom: A liquid bridge exerts adhesive force via surface tension (always attractive) plus Laplace pressure (sign depends on meniscus curvature), pulling two surfaces together.

atoms.verbatim_quote: adhesion depends upon the surface roughness which prevents the formation of a complete capillary meniscus at the particle contact point until a critical relative humidity is reached
atoms.mechanism_atom: Bridge formation is threshold-dependent (critical humidity/volume); once formed, pulling surfaces apart beyond a critical rupture distance destroys the bridge discontinuously.

atoms.verbatim_quote: capillary bridge formation can drive particle assembly into two- and three-dimensional clusters
atoms.mechanism_atom: Selective capillary bridges between particles with compatible surface geometries direct self-assembly into ordered clusters, mediated purely by bridge geometry and wettability contrast.

source_results.title: Pattern Formation in Precipitation Reactions: The Liesegang Phenomenon | Langmuir
Bifurcation of the Ostwald-Liesegang supersaturation-nucleation-depletion cycle

concepts.mechanism_summary: Liesegang rings are periodic precipitation bands that form when one electrolyte diffuses through a gel containing a second electrolyte. The governing cycle (Ostwald-Liesegang) is: diffusion raises local concentration until supersaturation exceeds the nucleation threshold; precipitation occurs, consuming reactants; this creates a local depletion zone around the band; diffusion must replenish the depleted zone before supersaturation can build again at a more distant location; the next band precipitates further out; geometric spacing (Jablczynski spacing law) and the width law emerge from the interplay of diffusion rate and depletion radius. No convection is required; the pattern is entirely diffusion-reaction driven.

atoms.verbatim_quote: supersaturation is so high that precipitation occurs immediately, and this process decreases the local concentration much faster than diffusion can increase it, inducing a diffusion flux from nearby regions and depleting the inner electrolyte in the precipitation band surroundings
atoms.mechanism_atom: When local reactant concentration exceeds the nucleation supersaturation threshold, precipitation fires and immediately depletes the surrounding zone, creating a refractory gap before the next band can nucleate.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the band formation emerges from the coupling of diffusion to the precipitation reaction, and was first explained based on a repetitive scenario of supersaturation, nucleation and depletion, the so-called Ostwald cycle
atoms.mechanism_atom: Diffusion-reaction coupling produces geometrically increasing inter-band spacing: each depletion zone must be replenished by diffusion before the wavefront can trigger the next nucleation event.

atoms.verbatim_quote: diffusion of reactants leads to supersaturation and nucleation; this precipitation results in localized band formation and depletion of reactants in adjacent zones
atoms.mechanism_atom: The precipitation wavefront propagates outward through gel; each band event locally resets the concentration field, advancing the active front stepwise while leaving behind a periodic record.

source_results.title: Turbidity currents and turbidites - Geology is the Way
Turbidity Current - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics

concepts.mechanism_summary: A turbidity current is a density-driven underflow: suspended sediment increases the bulk density of the water-sediment mixture above that of the surrounding ambient water; gravity then drives the denser mixture downslope along the seafloor or lake bottom. Crucially, the turbulence generated by the flow keeps sediment in suspension, which maintains the density excess, which sustains the flow — a self-reinforcing autosuspension feedback. The current decelerates when the slope decreases, losing turbulence; sediment drops out in a systematic fining-upward Bouma sequence (gravel → sand → silt → clay from base to top). Triggers include earthquakes, slope failure, or storm resuspension.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the driving force behind a turbidity current is gravity acting on the high density of the sediments temporarily suspended within a fluid, with semi-suspended solids making the average density of the sediment-bearing water greater than that of the surrounding, undisturbed water
atoms.mechanism_atom: Gravity acts on suspended-sediment-enhanced density excess; the denser mixture flows downslope as a coherent underflow beneath lighter ambient water.

atoms.verbatim_quote: autosuspension is a feedback mechanism in active turbidity currents whereby turbulence maintains the suspended load; the suspended load causes the high density of the suspension; the high density of the suspension causes the flow; and the flow causes turbulence
atoms.mechanism_atom: Self-reinforcing positive feedback loop: flow generates turbulence → turbulence suspends sediment → suspended sediment elevates density → density excess drives flow. The current can travel hundreds of km without external energy input.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the sediment-laden flow must generate enough turbulence to hold the sediment in suspension
atoms.mechanism_atom: When turbulence falls below the threshold to support suspension, sediment drops out in grain-size order (Bouma sequence), recording the deceleration history of the current as a graded deposit.

source_results.title: Varves in lacustrine sediments - a review | ScienceDirect

concepts.mechanism_summary: Varves are annual sediment couplets preserved in glaciolacustrine settings. Each couplet consists of a coarser, lighter-colored summer layer (silt to fine sand delivered by high-energy glacial meltwater) overlying a finer, darker winter layer (clay-sized particles that settle slowly through still, ice-covered water). The alternation requires: (1) a strong seasonal forcing of input energy and particle size; (2) anoxic bottom conditions that prevent bioturbation; (3) absence of full water-column mixing that would resuspend settled fine material. Finer particles settle last due to lower Stokes settling velocity. The annual couplet is preserved intact because nothing disturbs the bottom after deposition.

atoms.verbatim_quote: a varve is a distinct annual layer of sediment deposited in a body of water, typically consisting of a couplet of contrasting layers: a coarser, lighter-colored summer sublayer formed by seasonal influxes of meltwater and coarser particles, and a finer, darker winter layer resulting from reduced sedimentation during periods of ice cover or low flow
atoms.mechanism_atom: Seasonal energy forcing stratifies each annual deposit into a coarse/fine couplet: high-energy summer input deposits silt; quiescent winter allows only clay-sized particles to settle, recording the year's cycle in grain-size contrast.

atoms.verbatim_quote: varve formation requires the absence of bioturbation, and consequently, varves commonly form under anoxic conditions
atoms.mechanism_atom: Anoxic bottom-water conditions eliminate burrowing organisms; the absence of bioturbation preserves the lamination intact, enabling faithful recording of the annual cycle without physical erasure.

atoms.verbatim_quote: the finest sediments, the clays, flocculate in the water column and settle out of suspension in the lake during winter
atoms.mechanism_atom: Differential settling velocity (Stokes law) separates particle sizes in time: coarse particles settle fast in summer, fine clays settle extremely slowly and only reach the bottom in still winter water — creating the characteristic size grading within each couplet.

source_results.title: Patterned ground - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
PERIGLACIAL LANDFORMS | Patterned Ground | Request PDF

concepts.mechanism_summary: Patterned ground (sorted circles, polygons, stripes) forms in periglacial environments through repeated freeze-thaw cycles that differentially heave soil particles. When the active layer freezes downward, ice lenses form preferentially in fine-grained soils (higher water retention), lifting fine material more than coarse material (differential frost heave). As the ground thaws, this differential displacement is not fully reversed. Over many cycles, a positive feedback develops: coarse stones progressively migrate to the perimeter of fine-grained circles through a combination of frost heave ejection and convection-like cryoturbation. The wavelength (circle diameter) is set by the balance between frost-heave forcing and soil viscous resistance, forming self-organized geometric patterns on scales of centimeters to meters.

atoms.verbatim_quote: repeated cycles of freezing and thawing cause the differential movement and sorting of soil particles, stones, and finer sediments based on size and density; ice expansion during freezing heaves coarser materials upward and outward, while finer particles migrate downward or to the centers
atoms.mechanism_atom: Differential frost heave: fine soils expand more on freezing (more water retained, more ice formed) than coarse soils; coarser stones are preferentially pushed upward and outward, initiating spatial sorting.

atoms.verbatim_quote: sorted soil circles develop from a convection-like circulation of soil in the active layer of permafrost
atoms.mechanism_atom: A convection-like cryoturbation cell develops: fine material rises in circle centers; coarser stones accumulate at the cell margins; the circulation reinforces itself over many freeze-thaw cycles to form stable sorted polygons.

atoms.verbatim_quote: most patterns evolve through differential frost heave that develops a stable wavelength through self-regulating feedback processes and/or buoyancy-driven soil circulation
atoms.mechanism_atom: The system self-organizes to a characteristic wavelength determined by the balance between frost-heave forcing and viscous resistance; once established, the pattern is stable and self-reinforcing.
